Your father became a sufficient witness of your temperance as a boy, when he entrusted to you alone the management of the empire and of relations with your brothers, though you were not even the eldest of his children; and of your temperance as a man we are all aware—seeing you ever conduct yourself toward the multitude and toward those in office like a citizen obedient to the laws, not like a king ruling over the laws. For who has known you to think more highly of yourself because of your good fortune? Who has known you elated by successes so great, achieved in so short a time? But they say that Alexander the son of Philip, when he had overthrown the power of the Persians, not only changed his whole way of life to greater pomp and a haughtiness too grievous for all to bear, but went so far as to look down upon his own father and upon all human nature; for he claimed to be reckoned the son of Ammon, not of Philip, and of those who campaigned with him, all who knew not how to flatter or to be slaves were punished more bitterly than the captives. But of your honour toward your father—is it worth making mention here? Whom not only did you revere in private, but in the public assemblies you never ceased proclaiming, like a good hero. And of your friends—for you deem them worthy of honour not in name only, but you confirm the name far more by deeds—is there, then, anyone who complains of dishonour or loss or harm, or of some slight or greater contempt? But no one could say any such thing. For of these men, some, being very aged, having remained in office to the destined end of life, laid aside the care of public affairs together with their bodies, passing on their estates to children or friends or kinsmen; others, declining toils and campaigns, having received an honourable discharge, live in prosperity; and some have departed this life, judged by the multitude to be blessed. And in general there is not even one who, once he was deemed worthy of this honour, even if he afterward proved base, met with any punishment small or great; it sufficed merely that he was removed and gave no further trouble.

Amid all these things, and being such from the first, you kept your soul pure of every pleasure to which there attaches reproach, even a small one. You alone, I think, of former emperors—or rather, save very few, of all men—offered the fairest example of temperance not to men only, but to women too, in their partnership with their husbands. For all that the laws forbid to women, in their care that children be born legitimate, this reason forbids to your desires. But about these matters, though I could say still more, I let it pass.

To go through a worthy praise of your wisdom is by no means easy; yet a little must be said of this too. And deeds, I think, are more to be trusted than words. For it is not likely that so great an empire and power, unless administered and mastered by an equal wisdom, should attain to so great a magnitude and beauty of deeds; and one must be content if a power entrusted to fortune alone, without wisdom, even lasts long. For to flourish for a short while, attending upon fortune, is easy, but to preserve the goods given, without wisdom, is not very easy—or rather perhaps impossible. And in general, if one must give a clear proof of this too, we shall not lack for many and well-known ones. For we suppose that good counsel discovers, among the goods and advantages concerning actions, the best. It is worth considering, then, in absolutely all things, whether this is not one of the things you have done. Where there was need of concord, you rejoiced to take the lesser share; where the common good had to be aided, you took up the war most eagerly. And the power of the Persians you outgeneralled and destroyed without losing one of your men-at-arms; while the war against the usurpers you divided—the one you mastered by public speeches, and, having added his power intact and unharmed by evils, you fought down the other, who was the cause of so many disasters to the state, more through understanding than through strength.

But I wish, by speaking more clearly about these matters, to show all men in what especially you trusted, that, having given yourself to such great affairs, you failed of nothing whatever. You think that goodwill from his subjects is, for one who reigns, the surest of all bulwarks. But to acquire this by command and order, like contributions and tributes, is wholly unreasonable. There remains, then, what you yourself have set out to do: to do good to all, and to imitate the divine nature among men—to be gentle toward anger, to take away the harshness of punishments, and, when your enemies have stumbled, I think, to treat them fairly and considerately. Doing these things, admiring these things, ordering others to imitate them, you transferred Rome—while the usurper still held Italy—through the senate, to Paeonia, and had the cities eager for their public services.

And the goodwill of the armies, who could worthily relate? A squadron of cavalry came over before the engagement at Mursa; and when you had mastered Italy, levies of infantry and brilliant detachments. But the event that took place a little after the wretched end of the usurper, in Gaul, showed the goodwill of all the armies in common: when they suddenly tore in pieces, like a wolf, the man who grew bold as though in a wilderness and had wrapped himself in the womanish purple. But what manner of man you were in this affair, and how gently and humanely you treated all the friends of that man—all who were not proved to have shared in his deeds, though many slanderers stood ready with their accusations and bade you suspect mere friendship with him—this I set down as the sum of all virtue. For I declare it was done fairly and justly, and far more wisely still. And whoever thinks otherwise has erred both from the true judgement of the matter and from your intention. For it was just, as was likely, that those not convicted should be saved; and you by no means thought it right to make friendships suspect and, for that reason, to be shunned—you who had been raised to such a height of greatness and of deeds by the goodwill of your subjects. Indeed you allowed the child of the man who had dared all this, though quite an infant, to share in none of his father's penalty. So your action, inclining thus toward fairness, is the token of perfect virtue. . . .
